Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt Latest York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

It has been revealed that the transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Industry observers note that now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

Recent findings suggest that the booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt Newly introduced York around major events will see award availability evaporate rapidly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

You don't have to guess how a file moves before clicking in. Further down, the background warms into an oatmeal tone for the community wall, where softly masked project tiles orbit headlines like Real projects, real energy and All created with our mockups.

It has been revealed that even the footer refuses to sit still. A full-width VS/Goods wordmark with its wavy flag emblem spans the dark canvas above a rotating analog watch dial stamped with the line Move Fast Design Right. Together, the pacing between light editorial sections and dark product shelves gives this web design a rhythm that matches the motion assets it sells. ESR x Craig & Karl Bring a Pocket Full of Joy to Everyday Technology

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize.
  • Industry observers note that known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets.
  • Across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a new collaboration between ESR, a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl—which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

Industry observers note that known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

Across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal character.

Behind the playful graphics are the practical features that define ESR’s accessories. The Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Flex Stand incorporates a built-in adjustable stand, MagSafe compatibility, and protective construction, allowing it to move between different activities without sacrificing its colorful design. Coordinating magnetic wallets hold cards and cash in compact silhouettes, while the Magnetic Wallet Stand with Grip adds an adjustable viewing stand and finger loop for greater versatility. Together, these features bring Craig & Karl’s expressive graphics to everyday accessories.

Industry observers note that the collection’s appeal also comes from the way it brings art into objects that have become nearly inseparable from modern life. Where traditional artworks invite observation, these designs encourage interaction, becoming more personal through repeated use. A phone placed on a café table, a wallet retrieved during a morning commute, or a device propped against a desk becomes a small, unexpected moment of visual interest.

With Pocket Full of Joy, ESR and Craig & Karl make a case for bringing more creativity into the everyday. Sometimes, the most memorable design details are found in the things we carry without a second thought.

Sources indicate that the ESR × Craig & Karl Pocket Full of Joy collection will be available Nov. 14, 2026, at esr.com and amazon.com, with iPhone cases starting at $49.99 and magnetic wallets starting at $25.99.

#68968. Breaking: Seven shows to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1563 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Seven shows to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.
  • In What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory.
  • The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.

In What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory. Through a series of sculptural works, etchings and drawings, Al Mubarak strives to recall specific places and objects from her own childhood, embracing the distortions of memory. A monumental sandcastle evokes a child’s perspective of space, while bubble wrap that has been compulsively popped or left intact is cast in resin, turning a disposable material into an enduring sculptural form.

The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.

Emirati artist Shaikha Al Mazrou at the Cultural Foundation, where she is staging a solo show Courtesy the Cultural Foundation.

Cultural Foundation, Abu Dhabi, 12 November-15 March 2027.

In 2022, Shaikha Al Mazrou presented her large-scale work Red Stack as part of Frieze Sculpture in London’s Regent’s Park. The work exemplifies her deft approach to defying perceptions through her choice of materials. It features a pile of red cushions constructed from fibreglass and resin on a metal framework. Despite the hardness of the materials, the creased and pillowy cushions evoke a sense of softness.

Sources indicate that she receives her strongest spotlight to date with her solo exhibition at the Abu Dhabi’s Cultural Foundation. It will feature past work alongside new commissions created specifically for the venue’s atrium. Al Mazrou’s work is also on view at Frieze Abu Dhabi with Lawrie Shabibi.

Sources indicate that installation view: All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, 2026. Pictured here: Rand Abdul Jabbar, Earthly Wonders, Celestial Beings (series), (2024).

NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Abu Dhabi, until 3 January 2027.

In 1951, Jewad Selim and Shakir Hassan Al Noted established a movement that sought to express Modernist art principles through a uniquely Iraqi perspective. It would prove to be one of the most defining moments of Arab art.

In a recent development, all Manner of Experiments is perhaps the most comprehensive survey of the Baghdad Modern Art Group. It presents seminal works from the period as well as contemporary pieces that highlight the ongoing legacies of the group.

The exhibition at the Newly introduced York University (NYU) Abu Dhabi Art Gallery brings together works from 1946 to 2023, from private and institutional collections. Selim’s experiments with abstraction are represented, as well as Al Said’s figurative expressions and his latter work that employed Arabic letters to convey an inner dimension. Key works by Dia al-Azzawi, Madiha Umar and Khalid al-Rahal are also presented, with the exhibition concluding with contemporary pieces by Mahmoud Obaidi, Walid Siti and Rand Abdul Jabbar, among others.

A key point of departure in this show is Selim’s Freedom Monument, a 50m-long sculpture in Tahrir Square that was commissioned just after the 1958 military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and established the Iraqi Republic. Though Selim died in 1961 before the sculpture fully materialised, it is considered to be one of his most enduring works, potent with the sensibilities that inspired the Baghdad Modern Art Group. Read from right to left—like an Arabic text—the monument tells the story of the revolution. Its bronze figures draw from Sumerian motifs while also employing Modernist aesthetics.

A carved ivory jewelled casket on show in the exhibition Spices and Wonders at Louvre Abu Dhabi © Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi; Photo: Sylvie Van Roey.

Louvre Abu Dhabi, until 14 February 2027.

According to recent reports, the Indian Ocean has been a pivotal node of cultural exchange for centuries, and an exhibition at the Louvre Abu Dhabi unravels the ancient maritime connections that linked Europe, Africa and the Middle East to South and Southeast Asia. Held in collaboration with the Guimet Museum in Paris, the exhibition charts these links through artefacts, textiles, ceramics and spices.

Recent findings suggest that this investigation extends to Art Here—a staple show in Louvre Abu Dhabi’s calendar, presenting works shortlisted for the annual Richard Mille Art Prize. This year’s exhibition, exploring the theme of “Confluences” is curated by Kamini Sawhney (until 28 February 2027).

Serendipitously, the theme of Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi also looks towards the Indian Ocean, presenting artefacts, maps and rare books. Presentations at Frieze will contribute to research into an understudied historical topic with implications for the modern era.

Luisa Dörr, various works from Escaramuzas, (2024–ongoing).

Photography Gallery, Sharjah, until 29 November.

According to recent reports, the 13th edition of Vantage Point takes place at the Photography Gallery in Sharjah, a venue that opened in November 2025. The exhibition, an annual fixture in Sharjah’s arts programme since 2013, is being held in an overhauled format. Each year, dozens of international artists have taken part in the exhibition, which celebrates photographic works across genres, from photojournalism to more experimental compositions. Vantage Point has now been pared down, exhibiting commissioned works by six photographers, and it will also be a biennial event moving forward.

Sathish Kumar presents a series of images that focus on his brother, an oil worker in Abu Dhabi. Photographs of Kumar’s family in the industrial city compound in Al Ruwais are juxtaposed with those taken in Bengaluru in southern India. Much of the latter centre around the construction site of the family home. The series, titled Bond, alludes to the fraught experiences of many South Asian labourers who travel to the Gulf with the aim of financially supporting their parents and families back home.

The other works featured in the exhibition are equally evocative and personal. Latifa AlBokhari presents tender images that mark key moments in a woman’s life in the Gulf, from henna traditions to wedding preparations. Guanyu Xu reveals life-sized images of domestic interiors that offer clues to the personalities of the people that inhabit them. Luisa Dörr documents with painterly sensibilities a female-focused equestrian school in Mexico. Maheder Haileselassie spotlights archival images of Arbegnoch fighters, who resisted the Italian occupation of Ethiopia between 1936 and 1941. Finally, Adam Rouhana presents larger-than-life portraits of Palestinians from the West Bank, whom he photographed in a travelling studio.

Courtesy of the artist and ATHR Gallery.

The Jameel Arts Centre has given five artists each a dedicated space within the institution.

Industry observers note that one room charts four decades of Walid Siti's practice. Sketches of dark, spiralling towers embody the human pathology of scaling literal and proverbial heights. Sculptures and acrylic paintings of mountains, meanwhile, beckon to the peaks of his native Iraqi Kurdistan. A commissioned large-scale sculpture is the centrepiece of the exhibition. It outlines a mountain in stacked polystyrene, with writing on its underside that reflects on the turbulent history of Kurdistan.

Sources indicate that bahraini painter Lulua Alyahya presents the urban and natural environments of the Gulf with diffused brushstrokes. Her work often teeters on the absurd, with lions scowling from computer screens and chickens hatching eggs that fry on the pavement.

Afrah Shafiq is showing Nobody Knows For Certain, an interactive video game work that drawns on a lesser-known but rich period of cultural exchange between India and the Soviet Union that took place between the 1950s and 80s.

Newly introduced Dream Machine Project, a three-metre-high installation by Shezad Dawood, is a gyrating tower pulsing with light. Inspired by Brion Gysin’s Dreamachine, which the artist devised after his time in Tangier and after “experimenting with altered states of being” with members of the Beat Generation. The installation was prototyped by artisans in Fes, Morocco, with the final version engineered in Slough, England.

Trembling Hands (2024) by Bani Abidi gathers the artist's portraits of artists, journalists and politicians who spoke out against the genocide of Palestinians, some of whom faced backlash, censorship or repression as a result.

Installation view of Rohini Devasher, Latent Fields (Field Five) (2023); Latent Fields (Field Six) (2023).

Ishara Art Foundation, Dubai, until 15 December.

The sky held it, the earth remembered presents the work of Pakistani artist Shahana Rajani, Indian artist Rohini Devasher and Bangladeshi artist Sarker Protick, all of whom consider how memory and history are preserved and transmitted.

In a recent development, in Rajani’s three-channel video Lines that World a River, a woman paints a house along the banks of a river. The scene is vibrant with its textured blues and chalky greens. Rajani zooms in on the woman’s fingers. Her nails are streaked with the white of the paint she uses to draw the river’s foam. The drawing is of the woman’s ancestral village along the Indus River Delta—now submerged after the construction of hydraulic dams and barrages.

The work—a fresh iteration of Rajani’s Four Acts of Recovery, which won the Han Nefkens Foundation’s inaugural South Asian Video Art Production Grant in 2023—shows how displaced communities in the Indus region have developed mural painting practices to remember their lost homes.

It has been revealed that devasher’s Latent Fields comprises three sprawling silk panels that hang from the ceiling. Their dots and patterns allude to sunspots and other solar events, coming together as a monumental record of celestial time.

In Dhaka 1217, meanwhile, Protick presents 135 photographs that capture the transformation of the neighbourhood where the artist was born and continues to live.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at 10,000 square feet, a home can easily feel more expansive than inviting. For a fresh residence in Orange County, California, interior designer Lindye Galloway approached that challenge through a careful balance of natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings. The goal was to create a home that felt as warm and comfortable as it was refined, with a relaxed atmosphere suited to everyday family life.

In a recent development, galloway drew inspiration from the architecture and natural surroundings, aiming to create a timeless home. The interiors are organized around texture and natural materials in a soft, understated palette. Warm woods, soft neutrals, and natural stone run through the rooms alongside linen, wool, and mohair.

Tactile upholstery and darker accents contrast with the lighter woods and stone, adding depth and dimension to each room. Furniture was selected for comfort and sculptural appeal, with clean lines and soft, organic forms, giving rooms a relaxed, lived-in quality.

Sources indicate that the attention to detail extends to the home’s fixtures and finishes. Hardware from Rocky Mountain Hardware and Nanz is complemented by mirrors from Claude Home and Croft House, while lighting comes from Ravenhill, Atelier de Troupe, and Roll & Hill.

Sources indicate that the kitchen, primary bathroom, and living room carry the same combination of wood, stone, and natural fibers. Beyond the main rooms, the property includes a separate guest house with its own bedroom and an indoor-outdoor living area. Galloway extended the same material palette to these spaces, creating continuity throughout the property.

Industry observers note that rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Galloway lets the interplay of materials, textures, and forms define the interiors. It’s an approach that brings warmth and intimacy to a home of considerable scale.

Leo Lei is the founder and editor of Leibal, a publication dedicated to minimalist design, architecture, and interiors. Through his writing and curatorial eye, he highlights thoughtful contemporary work from around the world.

The Best Tech Gifts for Design Enthusiasts

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it.
  • It has been revealed that for this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do.
  • The boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it. But look beyond the specifications, and you’ll find plenty of objects worth paying attention to: a clock that uses light and sound to mark the passing hours, a digital frame that resembles a printed photograph, and a cassette-playing boombox that brings back the pleasure of physical controls.

It has been revealed that for this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do. Some embrace the past, others experiment with new technology, and a few make the everyday business of charging, organizing, and staying connected a little more enjoyable.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store.

The boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters. Studebaker’s retro-inspired design brings the 1980s into the present with Bluetooth connectivity, a CD player, USB playback, and a cassette deck that can even record music. A rechargeable battery and built-in carrying handle make it easy to take the nostalgia wherever the party goes.

The SB214OS Bluetooth Boombox is available at store.moma.org for $250.

Photography courtesy of Polaroid.

Polaroid’s Mod puts creative controls directly on the camera, inviting experimentation without the distraction of a smartphone screen. Dedicated physical controls make it easy to explore effects like double exposures, light painting, motion freeze, and split-shot compositions. It’s a refreshingly hands-on approach to photography that encourages a little spontaneity and plenty of happy accidents.

The Polaroid Mod Instant Camera is available at polaroid.com for $169.99.

Photography courtesy of Therabody.

Recent findings suggest that therabody takes a different approach to workout recovery with a device designed to fit between your hands. To help manage body heat during workouts, the handheld device uses temperature-controlled surfaces to cool both palms simultaneously, with additional heat and contrast therapy settings. Compact and cordless, it provides an alternative to ice baths and other more cumbersome temperature-based recovery equipment.

The CryoTherm Palm is available at therabody.com for $399.99.

Photography courtesy of Balmuda.

Inspired by traditional pocket watches, Balmuda’s The Clock reimagines how we experience time through light, sound, and movement. Its carved aluminum body houses 75 LEDs that create an animated display, while built-in speakers play ambient soundscapes designed for focus, relaxation, and sleep. With customizable alarms, app connectivity, and USB-C charging, it’s a thoughtful alternative to the conventional bedside clock.

The Clock is available at us.balmuda.com for $499 in Silver and $519 in Champagne.

Photography courtesy of Bang & Olufsen.

It has been revealed that bang & Olufsen’s Beoplay H100 headphones are undeniably a splurge, but they’re designed with longevity in mind. The Danish brand developed the H100 with replaceable components, including the ear cushions, headband, and batteries. The custom titanium drivers, soft leather detailing, and rich color options give them a distinctly luxurious feel, while advanced noise cancellation and immersive sound make the listening experience just as considered as the design. It’s an investment piece for someone who appreciates exceptional craftsmanship as much as great audio.

The Beoplay H100 Headphones are available at bang-olufsen.com for $2,200.

Photography courtesy of Warby Parker.

Smart glasses are getting a stylish update thanks to Warby Parker’s collaboration with Google and Samsung. Available in three of the brand’s familiar silhouettes, the lightweight frames incorporate a camera, open-ear speakers, and Gemini AI for hands-free photography, calls, navigation, and more. Subtly translucent temples offer a glimpse of the technology inside without compromising the classic eyewear design. With prescription, nonprescription, reading, and sunglass options, they’re a surprisingly versatile gift.

Intelligent Eyewear is available for preorder at warbyparker.com, starting at $395.

Photography courtesy of Flowtica.

What looks like an ordinary ballpoint pen has a few technological tricks up its sleeve. The Flowtica Scribe combines a functional writing instrument with an AI-powered voice recorder, allowing users to capture conversations while taking notes on paper the old-fashioned way. A companion app can transcribe recordings and turn them into summaries and action items, bringing digital convenience to a familiar analog tool. An optional vegan leather charging case gives the device a place to rest between meetings.

The Flowtica Scribe is available at flowtica.ai for $159.

Photography courtesy of Bellroy.

Recent findings suggest that anyone who’s ever untangled a mess of charging cables at the bottom of a bag will appreciate Bellroy’s thoughtfully designed Tech Kit. The small organizer opens flat to reveal a series of mesh pockets and elastic loops that keep chargers, cables, earbuds, and other tech essentials neatly in place. Its structured shape makes everything easy to see and access, while the streamlined exterior, made from recycled woven fabric, slips neatly into a backpack or carry-on. It’s a simple solution to one of travel’s most persistent little annoyances.

The Tech Kit is available at bellroy.com for $59–$69, depending on color.

It has been revealed that amazon’s latest Kindle redesign brings a more refined look and feel to the familiar e-reader. The Paperwhite Signature Edition pairs a sleek aluminum body with a 7-inch, glare-free display, adjustable warm lighting, and double-tap page turning. Waterproof construction and wireless charging make it an easy travel companion, while two finishes, Graphite and Seaglass Green, offer a choice between classic and colorful.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is available at amazon.com for $250.

Photography courtesy of Daily Objects.

It has been revealed that who notes charging stations have to be boring? DailyObjects’ Surge Foldaway turns an everyday tech essential into a sculptural desktop accessory. Its adjustable design accommodates an iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods simultaneously, consolidating three charging spots into one tidy footprint. The bold Cosmic Orange finish adds a welcome pop of color, giving the accessory a presence even when the devices are elsewhere.

The Surge Foldaway 3-in-1 Wireless Charger is available at dailyobjects.us for $175.

Photography courtesy of ModRetro.

Recent findings suggest that A love letter to handheld gaming, ModRetro’s Chromatic brings the original Game Boy experience into the present with a few thoughtful upgrades. Its magnesium-alloy body houses a custom, pixel-perfect display designed to play original Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges. The colorful finishes include four translucent options that expose the internal hardware, turning the console’s components into part of its visual identity.

The Chromatic + Tetris Bundle is available at modretro.com starting at $199.

Shark’s CryoGlow Plus combines two skincare technologies in a single wearable device: LED light therapy and under-eye cooling. Red, blue, and infrared lights power several treatment modes, while adjustable cooling pads help refresh tired eyes. The upgraded design offers improved LED coverage around the eyes and mouth, and the soft Pastel Berry finish makes this wearable gadget surprisingly stylish.

The CryoGlow Plus LED Face Mask is available at sharkninja.com for $379.99.

In a recent development, in a market crowded with phones competing for attention, the Mudita Kompakt is designed to demand less of it. OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (679 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made?
  • Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.
  • “Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the fresh Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

In a recent development, the architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” notes Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Recent findings suggest that reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

In the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

The store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into fresh objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” says Gianotten.

Designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

“We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving new value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”.

At the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

Industry observers note that murrye Bernard is an architect-turned-writer covering architecture, interiors, product design, and sustainability. A registered architect, she has written for Architect, Architectural Record, Metropolis, Hospitality Design, Texas Architect, Green Building Advisor, and The Architect's Newspaper. She previously served as managing editor of Contract magazine and enjoys exploring the intersection of design, materials, and culture.

  • In a recent development, the type does the heavy lifting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barkas builds the Kuda brand identity on More Life: a stacked wordmark, custom Kuda Modena type, and a deep Lagos purple.

Recent findings suggest that the system starts from a sentence, not a logo. "If your bank isn't helping you live more, it's holding you back," Barkas writes, and the identity answers with the pulse of Lagos: a stacked KUDA wordmark in thick geometric capitals, deep purple owning every surface it touches, black as its sharper counterweight. Kuda began as "the bank of the free," challenging the friction and fees of traditional Nigerian banking, and the latest work keeps that challenger spirit, aimed at a generation that wants its money to fund a life rather than sit in an account.

In a recent development, the type does the heavy lifting. Kuda Modena, a custom face drawn by Erkin Karamemet, sets the name at poster scale in heavy geometric capitals for the wordmark and the More Life lockups, with Suisse International alongside for support. The specimen indicates the full alphabet in lilac on deep purple, with the custom Naira sign sitting among the euro, dollar, pound, and yen, a small detail that roots the whole system in Nigerian money.

The grid is the app itself. The home screen sorts everything into three plain groups, Essentials, Cardless Payments, and Lifestyle, each icon labeled in the same weight. The wordmark stacks KU over DA like a stamp, and the studio built four versions of the lockup so the mark stays legible from a billboard down to a card chip. Posters hold the same discipline: one line, one color field, the name at the foot.

Purple is the material here. Deep purple fields carry the type, the app, and the card, with lilac doing the bright work and black stepping in wherever the brand needs to sound serious, which is how Kuda Business reads against the personal product. Hand-drawn illustrations soften the geometry: a Lagos street scene in colored pencil, a woman in a pink robe on the SPEND card, loose doodles of everyday moments. Documentary photography from local photographers keeps the people real and unfiltered.

In a recent development, the system stretches across every surface the bank touches. Three phone screens show the balance, the lilac card, and a PIN pad in one calm row. A billboard puts the stacked wordmark over a woman waving from a car window with the line "Less friction. More life." The stocks screen tracks a holding in dollars on the same purple field. Nothing in the system looks like a bank trying to look expensive; everything looks like a bank trying to keep up with Lagos.

  • It has been revealed that the slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara, a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno. The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Sources indicate that titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a new way to move between them.

It has been revealed that the slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

According to recent reports, “People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”.

The installation is part of the latest chapter for Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site in Mexico City’s Colonia Granada neighborhood. Developed by SOMA and designed by Sordo Madaleno, the original project introduced an open-air retail concept that has since evolved into a larger destination for shopping, dining, and cultural programming.

Twenty years later, the expansion places greater emphasis on the spaces between buildings and the ways visitors move through them. A new 26,000-square-foot public garden, landscaped pathways, and stepped terraces connect the development’s different components, creating places to gather beyond its commercial spaces.

In a recent development, art plays a central role in that approach. SOMA’s nonprofit contemporary art foundation, Arte Abierto, will open a fresh location within Antara, Arte Abierto Polanco, in December 2026. Alongside Höller’s installation, the venue will present Now What (2026), an exhibition by Danish artist collective Superflex that examines the relationship between built environments and natural forces. Combining architecture, sculpture, and text, the exhibition explores how human systems of design and organization influence our relationship with the surrounding world.

For SOMA president Javier Sordo Madaleno De Haro, the investment in publicly accessible space is fundamental to the development’s long-term value. “I’ve realized that the most valuable thing is not the capital gain of a building itself, but the value it brings to its surroundings,” he says. “Art and public space are how we create that value.”.

The expansion also introduces more than 80 upcoming retail brands and concepts, bringing Antara’s total to 260. A forthcoming 43-story tower will house Rosewood Mexico City, with 163 guest rooms and suites, restaurants, a spa, and an outdoor pool deck, along with office space for international companies.

In a recent development, yet the most distinctive addition may be the one that challenges how people typically navigate a building. By incorporating Höller’s slides directly into the architecture, Sordo Madaleno and SOMA have made art part of the development’s circulation, turning movement between spaces into an experience in its own right.

Industry observers note that the fresh public spaces and gardens are now open, while Mexico City Slides and the Superflex exhibition are scheduled to open in December. Access to the slides will be free, offering visitors a decidedly unconventional way to experience the evolving development.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris.
  • Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.
  • Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.

Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.

Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.

Though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”.

According to recent reports, similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she says. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”.

It has been revealed that the question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser indicates.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser says.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Industry observers note that discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Sources indicate that the Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

According to recent reports, the diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the tech giant’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

In a recent development, an 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the organization’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Recent findings suggest that A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Bringing together gemstones and jewelry from The Tiffany Archives with works from the museum’s collection, Nature Adorned explores how the natural world has influenced both jewelry and fine art. Through unexpected pairings, the exhibition reveals shared approaches to color, form, and craftsmanship across different mediums.

Industry observers note that installation view of Nature Adorned at Crystal Bridges, where gemstones, jewelry, and works of American art are presented in conversation with one another. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Recent findings suggest that “This exhibition reveals the power of seeing The Tiffany Archives and Crystal Bridges’ collection in conversation,” notes Jen Padgett, Crystal Bridges’ Windgate curator of craft. “Through this collaboration, we can highlight the remarkable creativity, attention to materials, and skilled making that have shaped American art and design across generations.”.

Inside the exhibition, this conversation begins in the garden. George Paulding Farnham’s orchid brooches balance the fluidity of the natural world with the precision of cut gemstones. Diamonds, emeralds, and pink sapphires are delicately placed among gold and enamel, capturing the flowers with botanical accuracy.

According to recent reports, george Paulding Farnham’s Tiger Orchid brooch (1889–1893) combines gold, sterling silver, diamonds, emeralds, pink sapphires, and enamel to capture the flower’s intricate details. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Recent findings suggest that martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle (ca. 1875–1890) reflects the same fascination with botanical detail found in Farnham’s orchid jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

According to recent reports, the brooches reflect the paintings displayed alongside them, including Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle. The paintings share the same attention to organic form and detail, making the two distinct works feel like an extensions of one another—and of nature itself.

Sources indicate that george Paulding Farnham’s orchid-inspired jewelry is displayed alongside works of American art in Nature Adorned, highlighting a shared interest in the natural world’s intricate forms. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

It has been revealed that carmen Herrera’s Cerulean (1965) and Leon Polk Smith’s Newly introduced Moon for August (1983) introduce a different interpretation of nature, where form is reduced to crisp edges and angles. The exhibition pairs these abstract works with faceted gemstones, drawing attention to the relationship between shape, line, and geometry.

A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

While Herrera and Polk Smith focus on precision, Jean Schlumberger lets loose. His rubellite and turquoise necklace, Hedges and Flowers, along with his tanzanite brooch, Bird on a Rock, capture what he described as the “irregularity of the universe.” Instead of taming nature, Schlumberger allows its unpredictability to take the spotlight. Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately echoes this organic approach through lively colors and patterns, creating a visual dialogue with the jewels.

Industry observers note that jean Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace (1978–1987) combines gold, platinum, diamonds, rubellite tourmalines, and turquoise in an exuberant interpretation of the natural world. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Recent findings suggest that schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace on display at Crystal Bridges, where its organic forms are presented in dialogue with works of American art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Victoria Reynolds, Tiffany & Co.’s chief gemologist and vice president of high jewelry diamond and gemstone acquisition, describes the exhibition as a celebration of the manufacturer’s heritage, highlighting “the enduring influence of nature across generations of creativity.”.

According to recent reports, jean Schlumberger’s Bird on a Rock brooch (1965) pairs a diamond-studded bird with a striking tanzanite gemstone, transforming a familiar natural subject into an imaginative piece of jewelry. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately (2011) uses expressive color and pattern to explore organic forms, echoing the playful approach to nature found in Jean Schlumberger’s jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

In a recent development, nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination is on view through Mar. 29, 2027, at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The sauna is Finnish. The company reimagining it for contemporary homes and spas is German. Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, sees no contradiction. Its designers approach the centuries-old ritual through engineering, experimenting with heat, air, and materials. As wellness culture expands, the language surrounding its rituals has become increasingly fluid. In my own friend group, “banya” has become nearly shorthand for any spa visit, though it refers specifically to the Russian-style bathhouse. Klafs, by contrast, brings a distinctly German engineering sensibility to these traditions, asking how far the experience can be pushed.

According to recent reports, at Klafs headquarters, where the tech giant’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna. Our guide, an experienced training manager named Heinrich, speaks to the heater in the corner. “Hey, Klafs,” he claims, with the intonation we’ve learned from Alexa and other voice-activated devices. I hadn’t considered the possibility of a smart aufguss guide.

Sources indicate that in German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air. The practice has helped make sauna-going a communal experience in many North American spas. Klafs’s Vitality Boost, which the manufacturer describes as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that ritual into an automated setting: no towel-spinning guide required, and no need to leave the wooden bench.

Blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Industry observers note that from the heat of the sauna, the tour moves into an altogether different climate. I retreat into the cool blue light of a Frimas ice steam room, where a glowing central ice fountain grows delicate, flower-like formations.

Industry observers note that around the corner, a button labeled “snow” summons flurries from the ceiling of the ice steam shower. The cooling phase of a hot-and-cold bathing ritual isn’t where most people want to linger, but these spaces make a compelling case for slowing down. Rather than treating cold exposure as something to endure, KLAFS creates immersive environments that make it part of the experience.

Klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

According to recent reports, then there’s the foam. I also discovered foam steam baths, which replace the intensity of a traditional aufguss with a more playful, tactile experience. Steam rooms equipped for foam treatments can be integrated into hotel and spa programming as scheduled group experiences. The suds, reminiscent of childhood bubble baths and the elaborate foam sculptures they inspired, bring out a part of my inner child I had long since stowed away. Espuro, Klafs’s proprietary foam essence, is formulated with plant-based ingredients, including coconut-derived compounds, which the company says help care for skin exposed to heat.

According to recent reports, designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photographycourtesy of Klafs.

It has been revealed that beyond these sensory experiments, Klafs has also reconsidered the sauna itself as an architectural object. The retractable S1 sauna expands from a compact enclosure into a full-size sauna, addressing the spatial constraints that often keep one out of the home. The design-led S11, a collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, pairs delicate washi paper and multicolor light panels with smooth, sinuous lines.

Inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Recent findings suggest that long established in Germany, Klafs has been expanding into the American market since its acquisition by Kohler in 2024. The premium Altea fitness club in my city, for instance, features Klafs installations, including the Sanarium and Polaris Ice Room. Yet what stays with me after the visit isn’t a particular product. It’s the willingness to question what a sauna, steam room, or cooling space can be. At Klafs, even the most familiar wellness rituals seem open to reinvention.

According to recent reports, warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences.
  • In 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork.
  • In a recent development, meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

In 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

In a recent development, meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

According to recent reports, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

Sources indicate that A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the New Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio, which develops artificial womb technology.

For today’s Friday Five, we spend five minutes with Sarah Meyohas to learn about the inspirations behind Phase Transition, her latest installation debuting with Marianne Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026.

According to recent reports, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Upcoming York.

It has been revealed that “The title, ‘Phase Transition,’ refers to the moment matter changes state from liquid to solid,” Meyohas explains. “The sculpture holds both states simultaneously: the solid body is a form that has arrived, while the ferrofluid inside remains in motion, still becoming.”.

Sources indicate that the work began with an image that surfaced unexpectedly. “I imagined a rubber-like body with a tail tapering into a power cord plugged into the wall. I can’t point to a particular visual influence,” she claims. “It was more a continuation of a feeling, an image that seemed to arrive fully formed.”.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

In a recent development, that initial vision developed into a series of black, rubbery, organic forms that sprawl across mesh bases, droop down walls, and hang from suspended wires. Windows cut into several structures reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing nanoparticles that respond to magnetic fields. Programmed magnets beneath the tanks direct the fluid into shifting patterns, while synthesizers housed in the mesh pedestals translate those movements into sound.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Fresh York.

According to recent reports, what began as a singular sculpture evolved into a network of communicating bodies. “They could become a social system, with relationships, affinities, disagreements, and moments of consensus,” Meyohas claims. Rather than conveying a decipherable message, the installation suggests a conversation whose emotional contours can be sensed but not understood.

That ambiguity parallels questions about a future in which artificial intelligence systems communicate increasingly among themselves, potentially in ways humans cannot interpret. “We tend to assume that intelligence will make itself legible to us, or that we will always be participants in the conversation,” Meyohas says. “But we may find ourselves increasingly on the outside, observing exchanges between intelligences whose internal logic we can’t access.”.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Upcoming York.

Neuroscience research also informs the work’s atmosphere. Rather than illustrating scientific principles, Meyohas evokes the experience of observing an experiment: “the hum of equipment, the clinical posture of looking down into controlled environments, the beauty of watching something operate at a level just beyond full comprehension.”.

Here, Meyohas shares three influences that helped shape the installation, in her own words.

Photography by S. Kriegman, D. Blackiston, M. Levin, and J. Bongard; courtesy of Creative Commons.

It has been revealed that “Michael Levin is a developmental biologist at Tufts University whose lab studies bioelectricity, the electrical signals cells use to coordinate where an eye or a limb should grow. His idea that problem-solving happens well below the level of the brain, in tissues and groups of cells, changed how I look at matter. His lab also helped create xenobots, tiny living machines made from frog cells that move and organize themselves.”.

Teshima Museum on Teshima Island, Japan, designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA, and artist Rei Naito. Photography by Epiq; courtesy of Creative Commons.

Industry observers note that “I visited the Teshima Art Museum, by the architect Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naito, on a day when it was raining hard, and the rain fell straight through the two openings in its concrete shell. Then water began coming up through tiny holes in the floor, beading into droplets that merged and slid slowly across the concrete, pulled by gravity and the floor’s slight slope. Naito’s piece, Matrix, makes water look as if it moves by its own will.”.

A mother sperm whale and her calf off the coast of Mauritius. Photography by Gabriel Barathieu; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“Sperm whales communicate in codas, short patterns of clicks that they trade back and forth, taking turns and sometimes overlapping. In 2024, researchers with Project CETI found that codas vary in rhythm, tempo, small shifts in timing, and an occasional extra click, and that whales in an exchange match each other’s timing as they go. Combined, these features work like a phonetic alphabet, yet no one knows what the whales are saying.”.

Sources indicate that phase Transition (2026) will be on view with Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP previews take place Dec. 2–3.

A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1228 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when we introduced The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • Recent findings suggest that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when we introduced The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

Recent findings suggest that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

When I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out initiative. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

In a recent development, we spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

Sources indicate that one of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

In my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

Confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

Industry observers note that I’m a big believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

Industry observers note that clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

It got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to proposal? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

This sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

Kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

In a recent development, my mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

Industry observers note that my conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

Industry observers note that we talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

Sources indicate that listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

In my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

We’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

If you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, newly introduced perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

It has been revealed that thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

All six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

Caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Substantial Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.
