Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century.
  • The repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands.
  • Industry observers note that the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

Industry observers note that the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

The Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil.

According to recent reports, “This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, mentioned during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”.

Recent findings suggest that brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she mentioned. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”.

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

More than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

Branding: Hyundai Card Brand Identity by Wolff Olins

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (462 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.
  • Recent findings suggest that the card is the poster here.
  • Sources indicate that the system runs on a simple split.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.

Recent findings suggest that the card is the poster here. The Purple, one of the new card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip. The same violet bleeds into a painted field behind the card, so object and world share one color. Wolff Olins spent time in Seoul before drawing anything, talking with customers and young Koreans. More than eight in ten South Koreans in their twenties still live with their parents, so people define themselves through taste and through what they choose to carry. A card indicates something about who you are and who you intend to become, and that became the design problem.

Sources indicate that the system runs on a simple split. A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card. Around that core, each card gets its own world. The entry cards, M, X and Z, use a generative system of bright color and repetition, so no two faces repeat the same pattern. A type specimen sheet sets the grotesque in full, and the card specification drawing marks the 1.58 ratio every face must hold.

According to recent reports, scale does the talking in the applications. The wordmark stays small and bracketed while a single figure, 93 percent, fills a whole green panel, and the card faces run at poster size on street walls. The card ratio repeats across posters, totes and packaging, so the system reads as one object cut to different sizes.

It has been revealed that the physical pieces carry the same discipline. Modular packaging holds the whole range together: a grey box with a debossed Hyundai Card mark and a red peel tab, each card sealed in a protective layer that peels back to reveal its character. The dotted halftone on the Purple card reads as texture before it reads as pattern. The tote bag carries the bracketed wordmark on green, with a black band at the base.

Recent findings suggest that color is the flex in the system. Violet owns the Purple card, acid green owns the commercial card and the major figures, and black and grey hold everything together. The butterfly image shows what the generative color does when it leaves the card: the same violet, painted loose across a wing, with the pattern breaking into dots. Every card keeps the same bones and gets a different skin.

See more from Wolff Olins on their site.

A Practical Guide To Naming Things

📅 2026-10-06 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1225 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In a recent development, naming is hard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables.

Sometimes, the names we choose are too generic, so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific, leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look.

If you’re looking for some inspiration for naming HTML classes, CSS properties, or JavaScript functions, Classnames is a wonderful resource jam-packed with ideas that get you thinking outside the box.

The site provides thematically grouped lists of words perfect for naming. You’ll find terms to describe different kinds of behavior, likeness between things, order, grouping, and association, but also themed collections of words that wouldn’t instantly come to one’s mind when it comes to code, among them words from nature, art, theater, music, architecture, fashion, and publishing.

How would you choose the right name for a given color? Fortunately, David Aerne maintains a tremendous repository of color names, right now with 30355 unique color names, sourced from various references and 1000s of user contributions.

Industry observers note that of course, the repository comes with a color picker and name search and plenty of other color pickers as well. Tremendous work, which is also a fantastic reference to keep nearby.

Recent findings suggest that what makes a good name? Javier Cuello summarized a set of naming best practices that help you name your layers, groups, and components in a consistent and scalable way.

Industry observers note that as Javier points out, a good name has a logical structure, is short, meaningful, known by everyone, and not related to visual properties. He shares do’s and don’ts to illustrate how to achieve that and also takes a closer look at all the fine little details you need to consider when naming sizes, colors, groups, layers, and components.

How to build a flexible design token taxonomy that works across different products? That was the challenge that the team at Intuit faced. The parent firm of products such as Mailchimp, QuickBooks, TurboTax, and Mint developed a flexible token system that goes beyond the brand theme to serve as the foundational system for a wide array of products.

Nate Baldwin wrote a case study in which he shares valuable insights into the making of Intuit’s design token taxonomy. It dives deeper into the pain points of the old taxonomy system, the criteria they defined for the new system, and how it was created. Lots of takeaways for building your own robust and flexible token taxonomy are guaranteed.

Looking at what other people call similar things is a great way to start when you’re struggling with naming. And what better source could there be than other design systems? Before you end up in the design system rabbit hole, Iain Bean did the research for you and created the Component Gallery.

In a recent development, it’s a collection that includes plenty of examples for more than 50 UI components — from accordion to visually hidden — and also lists other names that the UI components go by. A fantastic resource, and not only with regard to naming.

Industry observers note that features often have low adoption due to poor discoverability. Feature adoption needs time — first the feature must be discovered, then understood, then tried, learned, and eventually built into existing workflow. Erin Gannon has written a helpful practical guide on how to make sure all of it happens.

According to recent reports, good names are driven by user needs and problems. They should signal the value or outcome of a feature (the job-to-be-done), and — most importantly! — tap into the user’s own language. So ask people to explain a feature in their own words and then use the words they use.

A wonderful example of naming guidelines for a complex multi-brand, multi-themed design system comes from the Vodafone UK Design System team. Their Variables Taxonomy Map breaks down the anatomy and categorization of a design token into a well-orchestrated system of collections.

In a recent development, the map illustrates four collections required to support the system and connections between tokens — from brand and primitives to semantics and pages. It builds on top of Nathan Curtis’ work on naming design tokens and enables everyone to gather insight about where a token is used and what it represents, just from its name.

If you want to explore more approaches to naming design tokens, I’ve put together a list of useful Figma kits and resources that are worth checking out.

Romina Kavcic created a helpful little tool for naming design tokens — from learning how they work and how to name them well to configuring your own naming structure with components, categories, states, and roles.

If you are looking for the right name for your product or service, Onym is a fantastic open-source repository that organizes tools and resources for finding names for brainstorming, vetting, guides, sprints, etymologies — all the way to cautionary tales and agencies that name things, as well as useful books to take a look at.

A quick-reference list of tools and guides for naming just about… well, anything, in one place:.

Recent findings suggest that the right name is the one that’s well-understood and used by the team and users. So much time is wasted speaking about the very same thing but in different dialects — the designer’s dialect, the developer’s dialect, the product manager’s dialect, and the user’s dialect. That’s what often causes frustration and confusion.

It has been revealed that so if you see low adoption, it might be merely because of the name. And pay attention to potential naming conflicts and put them in a backlog of things to address later. It’s one of those fine little details that can reduce frustration and confusion and help teams work together better.

We hope you’ll find these wonderful projects useful — put together by wonderful creators. A friendly shout-out to everyone sharing their work with folks to use and learn from! That’s one of the reasons why we truly love the web and people building and designing it. 💚.

In a recent development, at Smashing, we love the web. That’s why we publish articles and books, run workshops and events around everything web. We love seeing what we all can do to make the web more accessible and usable. We also love organizing and attending online events — with friendly discounts for large groups (5+ attendees) and schools and students. Interested? Just send us an email and we’ll sort it out!

#68877. Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2048 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

In a recent development, yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

Back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

Sources indicate that sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

Sources indicate that back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

Recent findings suggest that the same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses tech giant-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these newly introduced systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

After all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

The main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

Sources indicate that one strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more rapidly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

Recent findings suggest that but, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

Recent findings suggest that also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

Most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a latest tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

Sources indicate that that doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

At a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

They need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

But formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff highlighted their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a big downside… mistakes will be made.

Industry observers note that many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a upcoming tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

According to recent reports, what they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

In a recent development, this time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

Look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

Staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

Industry observers note that but too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

In a recent development, that remarked, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

Again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

In a recent development, today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

Take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are currently bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

Industry observers note that and that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

According to recent reports, that is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Firm data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

The instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it reveals exactly where the official tools are falling short.

According to recent reports, look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

Organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

Recent findings suggest that I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

However, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out fresh technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.

  • Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, said in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees). That is an increase of 55% from the same sale last November, which topped out at $54.8m ($67.3m with fees).

Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, said in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades. Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”.

Sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees. With just 22 lots on offer—the house withdrew Derek Fordjour’s Haberdasher, estimated at $350,000 to $550,000, at the last minute—14 carried a guarantee.

It took less than a minute and a half, for instance, for auctioneer Henry Highley to hammer Claude Monet’s La Maison dans les roses (1925) at $3.2m, matching the $4m high estimate with fees.

Claude Monet's La Maison dans les roses.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, the Modigliani, also guaranteed, sparked a ten-minute three-way battle, escalating from the starting bid of $18m to $28m in just a few seconds before slowing to $100,000 increments. A phone bidder speaking with Phillips specialist India Phillips ultimately prevailed over clients on the line with specialists Jeremiah Evarts and Kevie Yang, placing the winning bid at $38.2m ($44.6m with fees) on an estimate of $28m to $35m.

Industry observers note that the piece, dating from 1911 to 1912, is one of just 28 sculptures by the artist, and part of a larger series of limestone heads each titled Tête. The price, while impressive, failed to approach the $70.7m achieved by another work from the series at Sotheby’s Latest York in 2014, which remains the record for Modigliani sculptures. His painting record, $170.4m for the 1918 painting Nu couché—the sixth most expensive work ever to sell at auction—dates to the following year.

The evening’s second-biggest lot was David Hockney’s eight-panel oil painting David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which sold for $10m ($12.2m with fees) within its $10m to $15m estimate. The artist, who died in June at the age of 88, made the work in 1982. It reflects his experiments at the time with photographing a subject from slightly different, overlapping viewpoints to create Cubist-inspired collages, and marks Hockney’s return to painting after a period focused on photography.

Helen Frankenthaler's Seabreeze.

The painting, which was sold by the Joel and Carole Bernstein family collection, also boasts an impressive museum pedigree, including appearances at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Portrait Gallery in London.

In a recent development, rounding out the sale’s top three was Alexander Calder’s 1959 mobile Snow Flurry, May 14—one of the few works without a third-party guarantee, and being sold by the family of Brazilian art critic Mário Pedrosa. Yang caused some excitement when she raised her bid straight from $4.6m to $6m, a price no one else was willing to top. The total with fees was $7.5m, above a high estimate of $6m.

In a recent development, helen Frankenthaler had the sale’s top result for a woman artist with Seabreeze (1980), which went for $4.5m (with fees). Frankenthaler followed that up a few lots later with Peacock Alley (1990) $2.7m (with fees), right in the middle of its $2m to $3m estimate.

The night’s only bought-in lot was Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia (2005), which carried an estimate of $650,000 to $850,000, but bidding stalled out at just $500,000. The rust-coated painting features a polyhedral glass-and-iron sculpture mounted on the canvas.

David Hockney's David, Celia, Stephen, Ian, London August 1982 (Four Friends) (1982).

It has been revealed that and while Jackson Pollock’s 1946 abstraction Constellation did find a buyer, the work failed to meet its low estimate of $3.5m. Despite the current show of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner uptown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a provenance boasting the legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim, the work hammered at just $2.6m ($3.3m with fees). Frank Stella’s Port Tampa City, from the estate of the late dealer Robert Mnuchin, also hammered below estimate, at $2.8m ($3.5m with fees) despite an estimate of $3m to $5m. The orange canvas, in the shape of an eight-point star quilt block, dates to 1963.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, both paintings made the sale’s top ten list, slotting in at number eight for Stella and nine for Pollock, just above the second Frankenthaler. Other noteworthy results included Clyfford Still’s PH-589 (1959). Expected to sell for $4m to $6m, it hammered for $4.2m ($5.3m with fees) to an online bidder from Tel Aviv.

Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

📅 2026-10-20 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In a recent development, in design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design. After more than a decade of working in tech, he … More about Brecht ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, in design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine.

According to recent reports, as someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a substantial part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log.

So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is presently rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool!

According to recent reports, and my second reaction was: wait… where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system?

Because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible.

If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform.

It has been revealed that take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive, organic, and human.

On the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring.

Recent findings suggest that randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun.

To see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos. But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax.

Sources indicate that the random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5. It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop.

The formal specification looks like this:.

In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments:.

It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type.

The CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers:.

If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly.

In a recent development, the optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments:.

This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid.

In a recent development, normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square.

That’s where the caching key comes in:.

Recent findings suggest that in the latest spec, a bare dashed ident like --square-size shares its seed globally across every element in the document (which would make all cards identical). To keep width and height linked on a single element while giving each card its own independent size, the spec requires pairing it with the element-scoped keyword (e.g. --square-size element-scoped).

To see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size, guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness:.

See the Pen [Uncached vs cached random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e91-4bac-765e-b04e-a53636759163) by @utilitybend.

Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports:.

There’s also another function in the spec called random-item(). While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords:.

This can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to.

And now for the practical part.

When I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word?

Think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections.

See the Pen [Imperfection random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-157f-708d-a704-fa067114aaca) by @utilitybend.

Here is the CSS powering the letters:.

I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back.

Industry observers note that one quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience.

Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:.

Screen reader customers get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks.

Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it?

It has been revealed that I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline.

See the Pen [Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-c117-729f-9844-ddf19fc1fc96) by @utilitybend.

Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up:.

Notice the negative animation delay (--delay: random(-3s, 0s)).

Sources indicate that if you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm.

It has been revealed that we’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards… Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns.

It has been revealed that for dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that:.

See the Pen [Random card tilt [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e93-849d-72a9-9254-3f4305e58a34) by @utilitybend.

Here’s how I put that together:.

In the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future.

According to recent reports, here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll?

In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection.

See the Pen [Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e94-79c6-70b1-97d4-66b7c2d736b0) by @utilitybend.

Look at how cleanly this works:.

If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page.

Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow, .drift-fast, .drift-reverse, or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms.

With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines:.

See the Pen [Random() velocity scroll animation [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-4cbe-77bd-9128-685d2c75cc56) by @utilitybend.

calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions (1, -1, 1, -1), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo.

I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh!

By combining random() with filter: blur(), opacity, and scale, we can recreate that lens feel:.

See the Pen [All about that random() bokeh [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-fe50-76dc-943b-d75fcaf704e6) by @utilitybend.

Some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds.

Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work.

Sources indicate that but! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this.

Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion:.

If someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility.

Recent findings suggest that tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy.

Whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition.

We spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web.

I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun.

Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random().

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, so what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

Well, research shows that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

In a recent development, the findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, customers expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a upcoming page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

Many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

The rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

In a recent development, using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a newly introduced page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

Industry observers note that it’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow people to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

For accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

Arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

The safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

Sources indicate that but we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — reveals all options and allows consumers to drill down.

And if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

We hope you’ll find these wonderful projects useful — put together by wonderful creators. A friendly shout-out to everyone sharing their work with folks to use and learn from! That’s one of the reasons why we truly love the web and people building and designing it. 💚.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

Sources indicate that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

According to recent reports, it wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

In a recent development, the evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in May 1986 for $1m.

Gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

In a recent development, A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s Latest York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s Newly introduced York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

In a recent development, french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s Newly introduced York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Big name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively big price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s New York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

Picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

Sources indicate that the Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s Fresh York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Recent findings suggest that willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

In a recent development, one of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article said the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

According to recent reports, it hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s New York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Recent findings suggest that though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export complications, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

Industry observers note that “It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” stated Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Igor Nora builds the Parniera brand identity from silk and sculpted gold, with a bespoke typeface and a silk moth mark in pale yellow.

The idea is a collision the project calls Sculpted Duality. On one side, fine silk in fluid motion, pale yellow, soft and light. On the other, solid sculpted gold forms with architectural weight. The identity holds both at once: garments described as vulnerability and armor, built for a woman who commands the room with quiet power. Nothing shouts. The yellow field does the talking, and the black line work sits on it with total control.

The wordmark is a bespoke typeface drawn for the house. Thin, delicate strokes carry the lightness, while high contrast serifs give the letters their structure. The detail that holds it together is the ligatures: internal connective strokes, clearest in the N, I, E and R, link the characters the way woven silk holds a thread, so the name reads as one continuous piece. A construction frame highlights the letters PA on black, with guide bars and notes on the straight serifs and the joins between letters.

In a recent development, the moth mark works the same way. It is built from four overlapping geometric forms, a line drawing of the Bombyx mori silk moth, the living link between the Persian name Parnia, a canvas of fine silk, and the sculpted gold the house stands for.

It has been revealed that the system stays physical wherever it lands. The moth mark sits alone on a pale yellow tile, then repeats as a woven petal pattern in yellow, gold and tan. The brand book opens in a black ring binder: a yellow page carries the wordmark embossed into the paper, facing a white page headed "Essence of allure." The same yellow carries the shopping bag, the wordmark pressed into the paper along the bottom edge, with black ribbon handles.

At street level the system scales up without changing its voice. A tall yellow banner hangs on a red brick building beside a panel with the moth mark, and the closing collage pulls the whole world together: moth tile, beaded gown detail, patterned envelope, shopping bag, the wordmark on yellow, and the line "Presence without the noise." It is a quiet luxury, stated once and left alone.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

The critical distinction is probate. In states with expensive or slow probate processes — California, Latest York, Florida, and many others — a living trust pays for itself many times over. In states with simplified probate procedures (like Texas or Wisconsin for small estates), the cost advantage of a trust is smaller but the privacy and incapacity benefits still apply.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

It has been revealed that an irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:.

In a recent development, the federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

It has been revealed that for most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate blueprint.

It has been revealed that the remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:.

A will alone is likely sufficient if:.

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:.

Add irrevocable trust structures if:.

According to recent reports, remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate initiative.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific concerns or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

According to recent reports, A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

According to recent reports, without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

The living trust vs will decision is not about which is better — it is about which is better for your specific situation. For estates with more than $100,000 in probatable assets, especially in high-cost probate states, a revocable living trust saves thousands of dollars and months of delay while providing incapacity protection and privacy that a will cannot match. For smaller estates in simplified-probate states, a well-drafted will with proper beneficiary designations may be all you need. Either way, the worst estate plan is no estate plan. More than 60% of American adults have neither a will nor a trust, leaving their families to navigate probate without guidance, pay avoidable costs, and endure unnecessary delays during the most difficult time of their lives.

Tech Report: Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” says Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the newly introduced attribution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown. But not all Della Robbias were created equal. Scholars and collectors have long given strong preference to Luca della Robbia (1399/1400-1482), the founder of the dynasty, and his nephew Andrea della Robbia (1435-1525). Similar works by later Della Robbias and those produced by the workshop can come in a very distant third. For decades, Newly introduced York’s Frick Collection believed it owned a relief by the family workshop, dated no earlier than the 16th century. But now, after technical analysis and consultation with experts in the field, the museum has updated its Virgin and Child to a 15th-century original, likely from the 1470s or 80s.

“We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” says Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the newly introduced attribution.

In a recent development, the framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs. Fashioned out of buff-coloured earthenware, it has the Della Robbia clan’s distinctive white and blue glazes, with, in this case, traces of gilding. The work was first acquired by Helen Clay Frick, Henry’s daughter, in 1922 and spent most of the last century stashed outside the main reading room of the Frick Art Research Library.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

Llanes Serrano says the road to the latest attribution was filled with twists and turns, and an outright gap or two.

Recent findings suggest that the early American luminary in Della Robbia studies was the Princeton University art historian Allan Marquand (1853-1924). Llanes Serrano indicates that in a 1906 publication Marquand identified the work, then in the possession of a private German collector, as being by either Luca or “very early Andrea”. Then, in 1914, he decided “that it had to be Andrea”. After it landed in the Frick family collection and found its way to the library entrance, it went from being a Della Robbia, generally, she says, to a work by Andrea—a decision, she notes, recorded by a librarian, though who actually made the decision is not known. Later, it was outright demoted to “school of Della Robbia” and has had that lower-rung status since at least 2008.

Julia Day, who was appointed last year as the Frick’s latest chief conservator, thought it was time to take a new look at the work after attending a Della Robbia conference in spring 2025. “I just thought that we have this piece, and nobody’s really spent time looking at it,” Day says.

Llanes Serrano, who analysed the relief over the last year in the Frick’s upcoming conservation studio, states XRF analysisallowed her to move back the dating and place it closer to Andrea himself. “I took multiple readings on different spots on the back and front,” she says, of the non-invasive technique.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the frame of the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

According to recent reports, the process revealed the elements present in the glaze, and then she compared her results with other analyses of autograph Della Robbia works. This helped her to place it in the newly introduced 1470s-80s time frame, when the older Luca was giving way to the younger Andrea. Meanwhile, another clue was plainly visible: “The Christ Child is clothed,” she states. In later versions of the motif made by the sculptors and their workshop, she adds, it was more common to show him unclothed.

A few weeks ago, the museum moved the work away from the library, where it was out of view from the general public, and installed it in a damask-lined spot in the mansion’s first-floor Octagon Room, fresh from its makeover during the Frick’s recent renovation.

Day says this kind of conservation-guided upgrade is a rarity at the Frick, happening perhaps once a decade. The Virgin and Child is the only Della Robbia piece in the museum's collection, she adds.

Tech Report: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex

💡 Key Takeaways
